I get my conditioning primarily via bodyweight circuits. I do 10 reps of a push move, a pulling move and a leg move in a rotation until I am tired, breathing hard, heart is pounding, etcetera.

I am often told on internet forums that this is NOT cardiovascular exercise, and that cardiovascular exercise can only be determined by heart rate measurement.

People who tell me this both obviously have not done what I am describing and don't have the foggiest clue how cardiovascular exercise actually works.

I am also told that the fact that a given exercise causes me to breathe hard, sweat and feel my heart pounding is no indication that cardiovascular exercise is taking place. They are wrong, that is PRECISELY what that indicates, and weâ€™re about to see why.

Here is what happens during classic LISS cardio, such as jogging:

  1. You begin moving. This is carried out by the muscles in your legs.

  2. The muscles in your legs begin to fatigue. Stronger, larger type II fibers either fatigue out or are not recruited in the first place. Aerobic fast twitch fibers begin to convert glucose to lactic acid, which causes "burning" in those muscles. That lactic acid is converted back to glucose in the liver (Cori cycle). Slow twitch aerobic fibers begin to take over, and aerobic glycolysis and beta oxidation of fatty acids eventually make up the bulk of your energy expenditure. These both ultimately create Acetyl CoA, which is broken down into substrates for oxidative phosphorylation by the TCA cycle, producing CO2 which must be cleared. Oxidative phosphorylation requires oxygen, in its absence anaerobic metabolism resumes, drastically decreasing efficiency and causing local lactic acidosis.

  3. To accommodate that need, cardiac output increases and blood vessels dilate within the muscles to aid in delivering oxygen and clearing lactic acid and carbon dioxide. Eventually as body heat increases, blood vessels in the skin dilate to aid in heat transfer, causing flushing. Decreased oxygen and decreased blood pH drive the hyperventilation that characterizes exercise: CO2 acidifies the blood, and it is freely exhaled, decreased blood pH causes spontaneous hyperventilation as also seen in Type 1 diabetics entering ketoacidosis.

That's what cardiovascular exercise is, not a particular exercise activity but prolonged use of muscle tissue at sub-anaerobic intensities.

There is nothing stipulating that this aerobic use of muscles must come from any particular activity, such as jogging. There is no reason why doing dozens of sets of fairly basic calisthenic moves cannot provide cardiovascular exercise. There is also no reason why prolonged, high volume, low intensity weight lifting cannot constitute cardiovascular exercise. There is no reason an hour of grappling cannot constitute cardiovascular exercise. Literally any exercise can constitute cardio so long as it causes enough energy expenditure and activates the right metabolic pathways. I would argue that there is strong physiological reason to suspect that full body cardio would be superior for energy expenditure than cardio relying only on solely the lower body as you have more muscles oxidating fuel at once. I would also argue that it's better for recovery, as relative to jogging, joint and muscle wear can be distributed evenly across the body while achieving equal fat/glucose oxidation.

This was very well put - most certainly better than I could have said it!

I think that people that think you need to be doing something that can be replicated on a machine (rowing, treadmill, stair climber, etc) are just being stuffy really.

Some people think cardio has to be just for the heart and lungs and that lifting anything will cancel the effect immediately. You could probably convince them that hyperventilating is the best and purest form of cardio.

If you're lifting or hitting calisthenics, it's simply enough to just keep moving, or measure your heart rate between sets and make sure it's staying elevated.

Cardio for a sport that uses both upper and lower body has to include upper body movement. If you run all day and just do that, you won't have the stamina to keep your hands up in a boxing match. That's where shadowboxing in weighty gloves (not dumbbells), push ups, jump rope, cross trainers, etc come in. There's a localized training effect that makes individual muscles more efficient. High impact running is not something you want to do non-stop if you're not a runner. Better to switch it up with other modes of exercise from time to time and ignore the wailing of cardio elitists.
Conversely, some people think that circuit training, while effective cardio, does nothing for strength or hypertrophy. I've always been a bit confused about that.
